content: Boron is a chemical element with the atomic number 5 and the symbol B. It is a trivalent nonmetallic element that is commonly found in evaporite ores such as borax and ulexite. Boron does not exist as a free element in nature. It has a hardness of 3 on the Mohs scale and is a weak electrical conductor at room temperature. Elemental boron is utilized as a dopant in the semiconductor industry. Boron compounds are significant in various applications, including lightweight structural materials, non-toxic insecticides, preservatives, and reagents for chemical synthesis. In plants, boron is an essential micronutrient, but both deficiency and excess can lead to growth issues. Boron toxicity symptoms in plants appear when tissue levels exceed 200 ppm, while deficiency symptoms occur when soil levels are below 0.5 ppm. Amorphous boron is produced through specific chemical reactions and consists of boron atoms randomly bonded without long-range order. Crystalline boron, a very hard black material with a high melting point, exists in several polymorphic forms. The most characterized crystalline forms include α-rhombohedral boron, β-rhombohedral boron, and 50-atom tetragonal boron. Crystalline boron transmits infrared light and is a poor electrical conductor at standard temperatures but becomes a good conductor at high temperatures. Chemically, boron is electron-deficient, possessing a vacant p-orbital, making it an electrophile. Boron compounds often act as Lewis acids, readily bonding with electron-rich substances to compensate for their electron deficiency. Boron is the least electronegative non-metal and is typically oxidized in reactions. It shares similarities with carbon in its ability to form stable covalently bonded molecular networks. Boron is also used in heat-resistant alloys and forms polyatomic compounds such as B2F4. In the automotive industry, boron has been proposed as a means to produce hydrogen by reacting with water, which could then be used in internal combustion engines or fuel cells. Boron isotopes, particularly boron-10 and boron-11, are useful in nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Boron-10 is effective at capturing thermal neutrons and is used in radiation shielding and boron neutron capture therapy for cancer treatment. In nuclear reactors, boron-10 is employed for reactivity control and emergency shutdown systems. Depleted boron, consisting mostly of boron-11, is used in critical semiconductor designs to prevent data loss caused by cosmic radiation. Boron-11 is also a candidate for aneutronic fusion fuel. Enriched boron-10 is used in applications such as radiation shielding and spacecraft structural materials, where it can absorb thermal neutrons and mitigate radiation hazards. Boron mining and refining capacities are sufficient to meet global demand, with Turkey and the United States being the largest producers. Turkey holds approximately 63% of the world's boron reserves. Economically important boron sources include ores like rasorite (kernite) and tincal (borax ore), with significant deposits in California's Mojave Desert and central Turkey. Boron compounds have numerous applications. Sodium tetraborate pentahydrate is used in insulating fiberglass and sodium perborate bleach. Orthoboric acid is employed in textile fiberglass production, flat panel displays, and eye drops. Borax is used in adhesives, anti-corrosion systems, and other applications. Boron nitride is a material where nitrogen compensates for boron's electron deficiency. Boron reacts with ammonia at high temperatures to form borazole, also known as inorganic benzene. Boron compounds are essential in agriculture as plant micronutrients and are used in pyrotechnic flares due to their green flame. Boric acid is used in textiles and as an insecticide. Boron filaments are high-strength, lightweight materials used in aerospace structures and sporting goods. Boron is also used as a melting point depressant in nickel-chromium brazing alloys and as an energetic material in rocket fuels and jet engines. Boron compounds show promise in treating arthritis. The hardest boron compound, rhenium diboride (ReB2), is synthetically produced and can scratch diamond, ranking higher than 10 on the Mohs scale. It is one of the three hardest known substances, alongside ultrahard fullerite and aggregated diamond nanorods. Historically, boron compounds have been known for thousands of years. Ancient Egyptians used borates in mummification, and borax glazes were used in China as early as 300 AD. The element boron was first isolated in 1808 by Sir Humphry Davy, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac, and Louis Jacques Thénard, though it was not recognized as an element until 1824 by Jöns Jakob Berzelius. Pure boron was first produced in 1909 by W. Weintraub. Boron is found in all plant-based foods, and its nutritional value has been debated since 1989. Studies suggest that boron can reduce calcium excretion and activate estrogen and vitamin D. Analytical quantification of boron in food or materials is performed using the colorimetric curcumin method, which forms a red-colored boron-chelate complex called rosocyanine. Boron isotopes are fractionated during mineral crystallization, hydrothermal processes, and rock alteration. The isotope boron-17 exhibits a nuclear halo. Elemental boron and common boron compounds like borates and boric acid are non-toxic and require no special handling precautions. However, exotic boron-hydrogen compounds are toxic and highly flammable, necessitating careful handling.
